newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin split by divisions even with Wall gone.
newsitem.headline: Berlin split by divisions even with Wall gone.

text.p: Seven years after the Berlin Wall collapsed and the city erupted into an all-night celebration followed around the world, Berliners paid scant attention to the anniversary on Saturday.

With opinion surveys showing east and west divisions growing wider, only a handful of Berliners were on hand for the city's anniversary ceremony where officials placed a wreath near a border crossing that was the first to open on November 9, 1989.

That was in sharp contrast to the hundreds of thousands who jammed the city streets seven years ago to celebrate the Wall's collapse. It also reflected bitter animosities that have grown between the formerly communist east and the capitalist west.
None of Berlin's seven daily newspapers carried page one stories on the anniversary.

Even the B.Z. tabloid, which best captured the sentiment of the Wall's fall seven years ago with the banner headline "Berlin is Berlin again!", barely mentioned the anniversary and devoted its front page to a story about July's TWA plane crash.
"A lot of people in eastern Germany are disappointed because the hopes of faster changes have not been fulfilled," said Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt.

Wolfgang Thierse, a leader of the opposition Social Democrats, said it was alarming that the economic gap between east and west was now getting larger rather than narrowing and blamed the government for dividing the nation.
"It is disturbing that a growing number of people in the east are finding it harder to find something positive about democracy," he said.

An opinion poll of 1,200 easterners by the Leipziger Institute for Market Research published on Saturday found that 44 percent of the easterners agreed with the statement: "The seven years since the Wall has fallen have done more to divide east and west Germans than the 40 years before it".
The magazine said Reinhard Hoeppner, the prime minister of the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, had recently made that declaration to which nearly half the easterners agreed.

The newsweekly Der Spiegel said an opinion poll by the Emnid research institute that 47 percent of all Germans believe the differences between the east and west have grown larger in the last seven years, nearly double the level of two years ago.
Only 43 percent thought the similarities between east and west had increased since the Wall's fall, down from 59 percent two years ago.
Although most of the Wall itself was quickly torn down, the divisions between east and west Berlin are hard to overlook.
Berlin is still marked by sharply divergent voting patterns in the east and west, different food preferences, newspaper reading and television viewing habits and even language use.

Voters in the western districts vote predominately for the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) while easterners cast their ballots primarily for the reform communist Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS).
There are also strikingly few marriages between east and west Berliners.
Only one in 30 marriages last year were sealed between eastern men and women and their counterparts in west Berlin -- a mere 562 of the 16,383 weddings in 1995.
